introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 3 : dates de l'historiographie courante (traité de Wuchale du 2 mai 1889, dénoncé par Menelik en 1893, Amba Alagi en décembre 1895, Makalle en janvier 1896, Adoua le 1er mars 1896, traité d'Addis-Abeba en octobre 1896, invasion fasciste en 1935, libération en 1941). Les effectifs des armées sont donnés avec prudence (« de l'ordre de dizaines de milliers de fusils modernes », armée éthiopienne bien plus nombreuse que l'armée italienne) ; aucun chiffre précis avancé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent can the success of the Abyssinian resistance against Italian imperialism be attributed to the effective leadership of Emperor Menelik II?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Abyssinia (Ethiopia) was the only African state, besides Liberia, to keep its independence during the Scramble for Africa. Its victory over Italy at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896 was a turning point and has become a symbol of African resistance. Menelik II, emperor from 1889, is usually given the main credit. This essay argues that his leadership was very important, but that the success also depended on other factors: Italian errors, the unity and strength of the Ethiopian army, geography and international rivalries.

**1. Background.** Italy, a late-comer in colonial expansion, had occupied Massawa in 1885 and created the colony of Eritrea (1890). In 1889 Menelik signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy (2 May 1889). The Italian version of Article 17 made Ethiopia a protectorate, whereas the Amharic version allowed Menelik to use Italy's services in foreign affairs. When Menelik discovered the difference, he denounced the treaty in 1893 and prepared for war. In 1895 Italian troops advanced into Tigray.

**2. Menelik II's leadership.**
- *Political unity.* Menelik brought together powerful regional lords (rases) such as Ras Makonnen, Ras Mikael, Ras Mangasha and Ras Alula, and overcame rivalries between Shoa, Tigray and other provinces, by appeals to patriotism, religion and the defence of the country. In 1895 he issued a general mobilisation call. Empress Taytu supported him and took part in the campaign.
- *Military preparations.* He imported modern rifles and some artillery, buying them from France, Russia and even Italy itself, and used revenues from conquests and trade. He modernised the army, and organised supplies for a large force.
- *Diplomacy.* He played the European powers against one another: he cultivated French and Russian friendship and made use of British-Italian differences; he explained his case to the other powers by letters, thus winning sympathy.
- *Tactics.* At Amba Alagi (December 1895) and Makalle (January 1896) his forces defeated the Italian advance parties, and he forced the Italian commander, General Baratieri, to choose between retreat and battle. At Adwa, a large Ethiopian army defeated the Italian columns decisively, and Italy lost thousands of men killed and captured.
- *Statesmanship.* After the victory he did not march into Eritrea, which would have stretched his supplies, but signed the Treaty of Addis Ababa (October 1896) by which Italy recognised Ethiopia's independence and the Wuchale treaty was cancelled. This showed political realism.

**3. Other factors.**
- *Italian weakness and mistakes.* Italy's army was small, poorly supplied and divided; Baratieri used inaccurate maps and his columns became separated; he was under pressure from Prime Minister Crispi to win a quick victory; Italian officers underestimated the Ethiopians.
- *The unity of Ethiopians.* A long Christian tradition, a proud national history and the example of earlier resistance created a strong sense of identity, and many Ethiopians saw the war as a defence of their homeland. The rival lords were willing to put aside differences.
- *Geography and numbers.* The rugged mountain terrain favoured defenders who knew it; the Ethiopian army greatly outnumbered the Italians and was well armed.
- *External factors.* France and Russia (and others) helped Ethiopia with arms and diplomacy because they wanted to limit Italian (and British) influence; the other powers had no great wish to support Italy.

**4. Assessment.** Menelik's leadership was the most important single factor because he used diplomacy, arms purchases, unity and strategy to build the conditions of victory, and because he used the victory wisely. But he could not have won without Italian blunders, the support of loyal lords and a modern army, which were partly the result of his own work and partly of favourable circumstances. Further, Ethiopian independence did not survive forever: Italy invaded again in 1935 and occupied the country until 1941, which shows that the success of 1896 depended on a particular balance of forces.

**Conclusion.** The success of Abyssinian resistance can be attributed largely, though not exclusively, to Menelik II. His leadership united the country, equipped the army and used diplomacy; the weaknesses of Italy and favourable circumstances completed the victory. Adwa inspired later African nationalists and Pan-Africanists.
